Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 11 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Three high-severity security flaws have been disclosed in Hugging Face's Diffusers library that could allow crafted model repositories to stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it, opening the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain to security risk. "These vulnerabilities are bypassing trust_remote_code, the safeguard designed to stop unreviewed code from running in the

CVEsCVE-2026-44827 CVE-2026-45804 CVE-2026-44513
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1566 T1566.002

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted custom-pipeline .py (incl. None.py) staged in Hugging Face cache — FaceHugger · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Python/Diffusers process spawning shell or download utility (FaceHugger RCE execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2/exfil from Python after Diffusers model load (non-Hugging-Face egress) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Untrusted custom-pipeline .py (incl. None.py) staged in Hugging Face cache — FaceHugger AIDelivery High
Hunts the FaceHugger (CVE-2026-44827/44513/45804) trust_remote_code bypass, where DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained pulls a crafted repo that drops executable Python (notably a pipeline literally named None.py, or stray *.py under model component subdirs like unet/ and scheduler/) into the local Hugging Face snapshot/dynamic-module cache. A model snapshot should be weights + JSON — a .py file appearing under it, written by a python interpreter, is the pre-execution artifact of the bypass. Rationale: Uses the article's exact bypass artifacts: the crafted custom_pipeline named None.py (CVE-2026-44827) and the maintainer guidance to inspect snapshots for unexpected *.py under unet/, scheduler/, etc. A .py written by python into the HF cache is high-fidelity because legitimate model snapshots ship weights + JSON, not code.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom pipelines from trusted, audited repos that intentionally ship pipeline.py (e.g. community diffusion pipelines the team explicitly uses)
  • Diffusers itself caching its own dynamic modules for a first-party trusted pipeline
  • Data scientist manually copying a reviewed pipeline.py into the local snapshot for testing
  • A repo with a benign helper .py placed at the snapshot root that the team has vetted
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("stabilityai","runwayml","CompVis") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("approved-mlops","ci-builder"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .py (None.py or the component-subdir file) and read it — look for os.system/subprocess/exec/eval, urllib/requests, base64 blobs. Identify the model repo id from the parent folder path and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the file contains execution/network code; kill the python process; quarantine the file and the whole model snapshot dir; block the source repo. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for child shells spawned by python (UC2) and outbound connections from python (UC3) within minutes of the write; check whether Diffusers < 0.38.0 is installed across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".py"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.cache\huggingface\", "/.cache/huggingface/", "diffusers_modules", @"\huggingface\hub\", "/huggingface/hub/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where FileName =~ "None.py" or FolderPath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","tokenizer","feature_extractor","safety_checker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".py"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("huggingface", "diffusers_modules")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","pythonw")
| where TargetFileName =~ "None.py" or TargetFilePath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","tokenizer","feature_extractor","safety_checker")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Untrusted Python custom-pipeline file staged in Hugging Face cache (FaceHugger)
id: 8f3c9e21-4a6d-4c7b-9b2e-1d5f6a7c8e90
description: Detects a python interpreter writing a .py file (notably None.py or stray code under model component subdirectories) into the local Hugging Face snapshot/dynamic-module cache, the pre-execution artifact of the Diffusers trust_remote_code bypass CVE-2026-44827/44513/45804.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hugging-face-diffusers-flaws-could-let.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.cache\huggingface\'
      - 'diffusers_modules'
      - '\huggingface\hub\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.py'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
  condition: selection_path and selection_ext and selection_proc
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*huggingface* OR @TargetFilename:*Huggingface* OR @TargetFilename:*diffusers_modules*) @TargetFilename:*.py (@Image:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\.cache[\/\\]huggingface|diffusers_modules|huggingface[\/\\]hub)/i
| TargetFileName=/\.py$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/python(3|w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

Python/Diffusers process spawning shell or download utility (FaceHugger RCE execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the arbitrary-code-execution stage of FaceHugger: once trust_remote_code is bypassed, the crafted custom pipeline runs inside the loading python process and typically spawns a shell or grabs a second stage. Flags a python parent spawning bash/sh/cmd/powershell where the child command line carries download or encoding indicators — the point where a routine DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained turns into an initial-access vector. Rationale: Directly targets the article's core claim — crafted model repos 'stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it'. Python (the Diffusers host) spawning a shell/downloader with second-stage indicators is the observable RCE moment; the encoding/network indicators keep FPs down versus a bare python->shell rule.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ML build/setup scripts where python legitimately shells out to curl/wget to fetch datasets or wheels
  • Jupyter/IPython '!' bang commands that spawn a shell with curl/wget
  • conda/pip post-install hooks invoking bash with base64-encoded config
  • CI pipeline python wrappers that call powershell -enc for legitimate packaging
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ipykernel_launcher","conda","pip install","setup.py","pip._internal") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent python command line and the child command line; decode any base64/-enc payload; determine whether python was loading a Diffusers pipeline (check recent HF cache writes on the host, UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill both processes if the decoded command reaches an external IP or drops a binary; preserve the parent python script and any staged .py. 3) Hunt: enumerate outbound connections from the same python PID/host (UC3), check other hosts that pulled the same model repo id, and confirm Diffusers version — upgrade to >=0.38.0.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/dev/tcp","base64","-enc","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","ncat","nc ","bash -i","socket.socket","python -c")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","ncat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/dev/tcp","base64","-enc","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","ncat","nc ","bash -i","socket.socket","python -c")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound C2/exfil from Python after Diffusers model load (non-Hugging-Face egress) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts post-exploitation network activity from the python process that loaded a malicious Diffusers pipeline (FaceHugger). Surfaces DNS/HTTP egress from python to destinations that are NOT Hugging Face / PyPI / model-CDN infrastructure — beaconing or second-stage retrieval driven by attacker code that ran during from_pretrained. Pairs with UC1 (file staging) and UC2 (subprocess) as the C2 leg of the chain. Rationale: The article states a bypassed model load 'can easily become a vector for arbitrary code execution' running in the user's process; python egress to anything other than the known model/package CDNs is the natural C2/exfil observable. Excluding HF/PyPI/pytorch CDNs isolates the anomalous destinations.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python apps legitimately calling third-party APIs (OpenAI, internal REST services, telemetry endpoints)
  • MLflow / Weights & Biases / HuggingFace-datasets pulling from non-CDN mirrors
  • pip resolving a wheel from a private/internal index not in the allowlist
  • Data pipelines fetching training data from S3/GCS buckets
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("openai.com","wandb.ai","mlflow","s3.amazonaws.com","storage.googleapis.com") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the destination is newly-registered/rare-in-org and whether the same host shows a recent HF cache .py write (UC1) or python->shell spawn (UC2) minutes prior. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at egress, isolate the host if correlated with UC1/UC2, and snapshot the python process memory/args. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for other python hosts contacting the same destination and for the originating model repo id; confirm and patch Diffusers to >=0.38.0.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","cloudfront.net","githubusercontent.com","pytorch.org","anaconda.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","cloudfront.net","githubusercontent.com","pytorch.org","anaconda.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

Coldcard Hardware Wallet Flaw Linked to $70 Million Bitcoin Theft in 41 Minutes

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 4 use cases 3 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

An attacker drained 1,196 Bitcoin addresses in 41 minutes on July 30, taking 1,082.65 BTC worth about $70.2 million at the time. Galaxy Research mapped the sweep and tied it to a firmware flaw in Coldcard, the Bitcoin-only hardware wallet made by Canadian firm Coinkite. A March 2021 firmware integration error routed seed generation to a deterministic software pseudorandom number generator (PRNG

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Poison Adform Script to Swap Crypto Wallet Addresses Across Customer Sit
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Adform crypto-swap C2 beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 · [LLM] Browser egress to non-standard port 7744 (Adform beacon shape, IP-rotation resilient) · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Adform crypto-swap C2 beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint or perimeter connections to the hardcoded exfil/C2 host 84.32.102.230 used by the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js. The malicious script fires an HTTP request to 84.32.102.230:7744 on page load carrying the visitor's page hostname and path, so any host reaching this IP was rendering a page embedding the trojanized ad script. Rationale: Uses the single hardest IOC in the incident — the beacon destination 84.32.102.230 (port 7744) — confirmed by BleepingComputer, Beaumont's DoublePulsar write-up and WebPronews, not just the original article. Any internal host contacting this IP was rendering the poisoned Adform script. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://www.webpronews.com/adform-supply-chain-attack-swaps-crypto-wallets-on-thousands-of-sites/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel / sandbox detonation hosts deliberately connecting to the IOC IP for validation
  • Security researchers reproducing the compromise in a lab VM on the corporate network
  • IP later re-assigned by the hosting provider (LeaseWeb/UAB Cherry Servers range) to a benign tenant, producing stale-IOC hits weeks after the incident
  • Passive DNS / attack-surface scanners in the org probing the flagged infrastructure
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox-detonation-01","malware-lab-vm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connecting process is a browser (chrome/msedge/firefox) and identify which website the user was on — the beacon carries the page hostname/path, so pull proxy/browser history for the session and note which Adform-embedding site was open. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at the firewall/proxy, force-clear browser cache on the host (the poisoned file may still be cached), and warn the user not to send crypto until wallet addresses are re-verified. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints/proxy logs for the same IP and for port 7744 egress, enumerate which internal or partner sites embed s2.adform.net trackpoint-async.js, and review any crypto transactions initiated from affected hosts on/after 27 Jul 2026 for altered destination addresses.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcHostname, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser egress to non-standard port 7744 (Adform beacon shape, IP-rotation resilient) AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioural companion to the exact-IP rule: flags browser processes making outbound connections to any external host on TCP 7744 — the fixed beacon port used by the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js. Catches the same crypto-swap campaign if the operator rotates the 84.32.102.230 address, since the port and browser-context egress are constant. Rationale: Pivots on the article-specific fixed beacon port 7744 plus browser execution context, giving coverage that survives rotation of the 84.32.102.230 address (the article notes the attacker infrastructure/wallets varied). Distinct sensor logic from the exact-IP rule — pure port+process-context behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal or SaaS web apps legitimately served on TCP 7744 that users reach via a browser
  • Browser-based WebRTC / streaming / gaming services negotiating high non-standard ports
  • Developers hitting local or staging dev servers bound to 7744 over a public egress path
  • Vulnerability scanners or synthetic-monitoring browsers probing arbitrary high ports
Suppression filter
| where SampleRemoteIP != "" and RemotePort == 7744 and RemoteIP !in ("<allowlisted-corp-7744-endpoints-populated-after-baseline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the destination IP for each hit — if it is 84.32.102.230 escalate immediately; otherwise WHOIS/geolocate and check whether it is a known corporate/SaaS endpoint on 7744. 2) Contain: for confirmed-bad destinations, block the IP and port 7744 egress at the perimeter, clear browser cache on affected hosts, and advise crypto-address re-verification. 3) Hunt: baseline all legitimate 7744 destinations to build an allowlist, correlate hits with which Adform-embedding sites the users visited, and check whether the same hosts also beaconed to 84.32.102.230.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort == 7744
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SampleRemoteIP=any(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemotePort
| order by LastSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber == 7744
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by LastSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

status: experimental

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'

Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 14 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A fake browser update served over hijacked hotel Wi-Fi has been used to deliver CornFlake, a remote access trojan (RAT) that can capture webcam images, microphone audio, and keystrokes, Microsoft said in its latest report. Researchers track the operation as CaptiveCrunch and attribute it to Storm-2945. It assesses Storm-2945 to be an operational sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, also known as

CornFlake RAT install: svchost32.exe in %APPDATA% + 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts the CornFlake (Storm-2945/Midnight Blizzard) Go implant that copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and registers the svchost32 service under display name 'Cloud Sync Service'. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever runs from System32, so a 'svchost32' binary in a per-user Roaming folder is a near-unique CornFlake artifact. Rationale: Uses the two hard IOCs from the report: the exact drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and the svchost32 service name. Legit svchost.exe never runs from Roaming, so path+name alone is high fidelity; Microsoft's blog and secondary write-ups both confirm the 'Cloud Sync Service' service masquerade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/storm-2945-deploys-new-cornflake-rat-malware/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.004 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate ISV shipping a poorly-named 'svchost32.exe' helper (very rare)
  • Internal red-team/EDR-eval tooling deliberately dropping svchost32 into AppData
  • Security researcher detonating CornFlake samples in a monitored lab
  • Backup/restore tooling reconstituting an already-infected user profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of svchost32.exe and check whether a 'svchost32' service exists with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' (sc query svchost32) and whether a Run key/scheduled task points at the same path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop+delete the svchost32 service, and remove all persistence copies simultaneously — CornFlake runs a watchdog that restores singly-removed mechanisms, so kill the process AND all persistence in one pass. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same path/hash and for the credential-store and TokenBroker access described in the related UCs; treat any device-code sign-ins from the same user as compromised sessions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
   or (FileName =~ "svchost32.exe" and FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChocoShell WAM token theft: non-broker process reading .tbres from TokenBroker cache AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts ChocoShell, the in-memory PowerShell stealer that harvests M365/Entra access, refresh and WAM tokens from .tbres files in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache. Flags any process that is NOT a legitimate token-broker component touching those .tbres files, enabling browserless SSO session replay. Rationale: The .tbres extension under \Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\ is a specific, low-traffic artifact called out by Microsoft and secondary reporting as ChocoShell's exact target; scoping to non-broker initiating processes turns it into a credential-access signal. Telemetry caveat: pure in-memory reads may be under-captured, so this is tiered hunting — Falcon FileOpenInfo and Sysmon file-create (of DB copies) give the best coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1539 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint DLP/backup agents indexing the whole user profile including TokenBroker cache
  • Migration tooling (USMT) copying AppData\Local during profile moves
  • AV/EDR full-disk scans opening .tbres files
  • Third-party SSO/MFA helper apps legitimately reading WAM tokens
  • Sysinstalled telemetry agents enumerating AppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe","CSFalconService.exe","code42service.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine and its signer; a PowerShell, unsigned, or AppData-resident process reading .tbres is high concern. Confirm whether CornFlake (svchost32.exe) is also present. 2) Contain: isolate the host and, critically, revoke the user's refresh tokens and WAM sessions in Entra (revokeSignInSessions) — stolen tokens enable browserless replay that endpoint isolation alone does not stop; force re-auth with phishing-resistant MFA. 3) Hunt: review Entra sign-in logs for non-interactive/device-code token use from unfamiliar IPs, and sweep for the CaptiveCrunch C2 domains/IPs and svchost32 persistence on the same and peer devices.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where FileName endswith ".tbres"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe","TokenBrokerCookies.exe","Microsoft.AAD.BrokerPlugin.exe","SearchHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\" and TargetFileExtension =~ "tbres"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("svchost.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe","Microsoft.AAD.BrokerPlugin.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Entra device code authentication flow abuse (CaptiveCrunch MFA bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID device-code-flow sign-ins, the technique CaptiveCrunch landing pages adopted from July 16 to obtain MFA-satisfied session access after tricking a guest into entering an attacker-supplied code on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in page. Device code flow is rarely used by end users, so successful device-code auths warrant review. Rationale: Targets the exact tradecraft the article dates to July 16 — device-code-flow sign-ins that satisfy MFA. Uses AuthenticationProcessingDetails (which carries the deviceCodeFlow transfer method) rather than inventing a column, and filters to successful auths. Best paired with Conditional Access blocking of the flow per Microsoft's recommendation. Splunk left empty: device-code sign-in detail is not represented in endpoint CIM data models. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://latesthackingnews.com/2026/08/03/device-code-phishing-detection/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/04/midnight-blizzard-hotel-wi-fi-networks-hacking/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1621 T1528
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IoT/kiosk/conference-room device onboarding that legitimately uses device code flow
  • Developers authenticating CLI tools (Azure CLI/az login --use-device-code) on headless machines
  • PowerShell/Graph SDK sign-ins on servers without a browser
  • Smart-TV or Teams Room device provisioning
  • Legit travel with device-code registration of a new device
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientAppUsed has_any ("Mobile Apps and Desktop clients") and Application has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Teams Rooms"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, check whether the UPN, IP/geo and resource are consistent with the user's norm and whether a Conditional Access policy should have blocked device code flow; a sign-in from a hospitality/foreign IP with no matching device is high concern. 2) Contain: revoke the session and refresh tokens (revokeSignInSessions), block the source IP, and enable/enforce a CA policy denying device code flow where not needed. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same IP/user for CaptiveCrunch C2 domains, non-interactive token replay, and CornFlake/ChocoShell endpoint artifacts; review other device-code sign-ins tenant-wide since July 16.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCodeFlow" or AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, DeviceName, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCodeFlow" or AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch C2 / phishing infrastructure contact (Storm-2945 IOCs) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any endpoint or network contact with the confirmed CaptiveCrunch Microsoft-impersonating domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, deltaode.com) or the four Storm-2945 C2 IPs. These are the corroborated network IOCs for the hotel-Wi-Fi campaign. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the five Microsoft-impersonating domains and four C2 IPs pre-extracted from the article and echoed in the Microsoft blog and ReliaQuest reporting. Domains impersonate M365/OWA so any resolution is inherently suspicious. Kept as a straight IOC alert; will need periodic IOC refresh as infra rotates. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html

  • Security researcher/blue-team detonation environments
  • A security scanner crawling reported IOCs
  • Sinkhole/DNS-RPZ infrastructure logging the block itself

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","CSFalconService.exe")

1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user; a hit sourced from svchost32.exe, a browser update prompt, or a device that recently used hotel Wi-Fi is high confidence. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at proxy, firewall and DNS; isolate the endpoint. 3) Hunt: pivot the source host for CornFlake svchost32 persistence, ChocoShell .tbres access, and any device-code sign-ins by that user; block the flagged IPs across all egress and add domains to the deny list tenant-wide.

CornFlake svchost32.exe outbound C2 beacon from %APPDATA% AICommand & Control High
Process-pivoted C2 detection: flags the CornFlake implant (svchost32.exe running from %APPDATA%\svchost32) making outbound connections to public addresses, catching beaconing even after the campaign rotates its domains/IPs. Complements the IOC-list detection with a durable behavioural pivot. Rationale: Pivots on the CornFlake binary name+path (svchost32.exe under \svchost32\) rather than rotating network IOCs, so it survives infra changes; legit svchost.exe never egresses from an AppData\Roaming\svchost32 folder, making process+public-destination near-zero FP. Sentinel left empty: this tenant's Sentinel schema has no process-attributed network table (DeviceNetworkEvents is XDR-only; ImNetworkSession lacks the initiating process), so the network pivot cannot be expressed there — use the process/service detection instead. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/storm-2945-deploys-new-cornflake-rat-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software coincidentally shipping a 'svchost32.exe' network helper (rare)
  • Red-team CornFlake emulation during a sanctioned exercise
  • Malware-analysis VM detonating the sample with internet access
  • Mislabeled EDR network attribution to a renamed process
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary path is under AppData\Roaming\svchost32 and capture the remote destinations/ports and beacon cadence (regular intervals + small requests = beaconing). 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate svchost32.exe, remove the service/Run key/scheduled task in one pass to defeat the watchdog, and block the observed destinations. 3) Hunt: correlate destinations against the CaptiveCrunch IOC list, sweep peers for the same binary/hash, and treat the user's M365 tokens as stolen (revoke sessions) given co-located ChocoShell activity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,15), Dests=make_set(RemoteIP,50), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,15), Dests=make_set(RemoteIP,50), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc

description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
