Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) · [LLM] Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the core arbitrary-file-read primitive of CVE-2026-66066: a crafted upload drives an unfuzzed libvips loader inside the Ruby/Puma process to read the process environment and Rails secrets (secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc). Because libvips is linked into the app process, the read shows up as the web-app binary opening files it never touches at runtime. Rationale: Anchored on the exact read targets the GHSA names as the payoff (secret_key_base in the process environment, master.key, credentials.yml.enc) and scoped to the Ruby web-app process as the actor — that pairing is the file-read primitive itself, not a generic file-access rule. Confirmed via the advisory plus Ethiack and Flatt write-ups that the impact is disclosure of the process environment. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails • https://www.libvips.org/2022/05/28/What's-new-in-8.13.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately reading config/master.key and config/credentials.yml.enc at boot (normal startup — not /proc/self/environ)
  • Backup or DLP agents reading /etc/passwd during scheduled scans
  • APM/observability agents (e.g. Datadog, New Relic) reading /proc/<pid>/environ for metadata enrichment
  • Config-management runs (Ansible/Chef) reading /etc/passwd or .env files
  • Container init scripts sourcing .env files at container start
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("rails server","puma","bootsnap"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the actor is the web-app process (ruby/puma) and the read occurred mid-request (not at process start) — correlate the read timestamp against Active Storage variant/representation requests in the web/access log. 2) Contain: if /proc/self/environ or /etc/passwd was read by the app process, treat secret_key_base and every env-resident credential as exposed — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB creds and S3/GCS/Azure Active Storage keys immediately (invalidates sessions). 3) Hunt: check for follow-on ruby-spawned shells and outbound connections from the host, and search web logs for the uploads that preceded the read (/rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads).
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileAccessed"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/proc/self/environ","/environ","/etc/passwd","/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc","/.env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/(ruby|puma|passenger|rails)/i
| TargetFileName=/(\/proc\/self\/environ|\/proc\/\d+\/environ|\/etc\/passwd|\/config\/master\.key|\/config\/credentials\.yml\.enc|\/\.env)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the RCE stage of CVE-2026-66066: after leaking secret_key_base, the attacker forges a signed/encrypted Rails cookie carrying a deserialization payload, yielding code execution inside the app process. Surfaces the anomalous child — an interactive shell or download tool spawned by the Ruby/Puma web worker. Rationale: The advisory states the file-read escalates to RCE via secrets in the process environment; the observable outcome is the Rails worker (ruby/puma/passenger) spawning a shell or fetch tool — a parent→child pair that is abnormal for a web app running the in-process :vips processor. Parents and children are all concrete binary names, no placeholders. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails apps that legitimately shell out via system()/backticks (e.g. running git, imagemagick/mini_magick, ffmpeg, or a rake task)
  • Deploy/boot scripts where puma is launched by a shell wrapper and re-execs sh
  • Health-check or cron jobs invoking curl/wget from within the app container
  • Background job workers (Sidekiq/Resque under ruby) shelling out to CLI tools by design
  • Container entrypoints where bundle exec spawns sh for pre-boot hooks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i ","sh -c","bash -c","-c 'curl","-c \"curl","base64 -d") or ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("git","convert","mogrify","ffmpeg","rake")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp, -i, bash -c with piped curl) or interactive shells with no args are high-confidence; benign shell-outs name a specific tool/arg. Correlate against UC1 file-read hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host/pod, kill the offending Ruby worker, and rotate secret_key_base + all env-resident credentials (the RCE path depends on the leaked signing key). 3) Hunt: pull the preceding web requests to /rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, review outbound connections from the host, and check for persistence (cron, authorized_keys, new services).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","ruby3.2","ruby3.3","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt for the attack surface: hosts with an activestorage version affected by CVE-2026-66066 (< 7.2.3.2, 8.0.x < 8.0.5.1, 8.1.x < 8.1.3.1), prioritising internet-facing systems and those still on libvips < 8.13 which cannot block unfuzzed loaders. Drives patch/mitigation before the 2026-08-28 full disclosure. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the vendor-published affected-version boundaries from the advisory; joining internet-facing status turns a raw inventory list into a ranked remediation queue for the specific gem in this CVE. No version-string math needed — the TVM CveId already encodes the affected ranges. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 7.2.3.2 / 8.0.5.1 / 8.1.3.1 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale)
  • Apps that carry ruby-vips only for image analysis and never generate variants (lower real risk despite matching)
  • Hosts where libvips >= 8.13 is present and VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true) is already set (mitigated without gem upgrade)
  • Non-production/staging boxes flagged as internet-facing by network heuristics but actually firewalled
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm variant_processor is :vips (default since load_defaults 7.0) and whether the app accepts uploads from untrusted users — those two conditions gate real exploitability. 2) Contain: upgrade activestorage to the fixed release and ensure libvips >= 8.13; where an immediate upgrade isn't possible, set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED=1 (or Vips.block_untrusted(true)) as an interim block, prioritising internet-facing hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that was exposed before patching, assume secret exposure — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB and Active Storage service credentials, and run UC1/UC2 retrospectively over the exposure window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc

Successful Entra ID device-code authentication (ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS MFA bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful OAuth device-code grant sign-ins in Entra ID, the flow abused by the ARToken/EvilTokens phishing-as-a-service platform to bypass MFA and mint persistent refresh tokens. Device-code auth is rare/unused in most tenants, so any success warrants review for account takeover. Rationale: Grounds on the ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing pattern named in the corroborated Talos IR Q2 2026 report; device-code auth success is inherently rare and high-signal for token-theft AiTM. Cross-checked https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-in from IoT/kiosk/CLI tooling (Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code')
  • Conference-room / smart-TV Teams device provisioning
  • Developers using device-code flow for headless service auth
  • PowerShell modules (Microsoft.Graph, Az) prompting device-code login on servers
Suppression filter
| where ClientAppUsed !in ("Mobile Apps and Desktop clients") or Application !has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools")
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each hit, confirm whether the user legitimately performs device-code logins; check the IP/geo/ASN and UserAgent against the user's baseline and look for impossible travel. 2) Contain: If unrecognized, revoke sessions/refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and re-register MFA; block the source IP. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the AccountUpn for subsequent non-interactive token use, new inbox rules, OAuth app consents, and mailbox/SharePoint access from the same IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0            // successful device-code grant
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0           // successful device-code grant
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized MeshAgent running outside its install path (Sinobi ransomware C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts MeshAgent / MeshCentral processes executing from non-standard locations, the trojanized SYSTEM-level auto-start C2 used by Sinobi ransomware operators. Legitimate MeshCentral installs live under a fixed program path; execution elsewhere indicates an attacker-deployed agent. Rationale: Uses the corroborated report detail that Sinobi deployed a trojanized MeshAgent as SYSTEM auto-start C2; anchoring on the MeshAgent binary/product plus a path-exclusion turns a legit tool into a high-fidelity attacker signal. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and detection.fyi renamed-MeshAgent Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/macos/process_creation/proc_creation_macos_remote_access_tools_renamed_meshagent_execution/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MeshCentral deployment installed to a custom directory by IT
  • Portable MeshAgent run from a technician's USB during legitimate support
  • Security-team red-team or RMM evaluation testing
  • MSP-managed endpoints where MeshCentral is the approved RMM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("approved-rmm-svc") and SHA256 !in ("<known-good-meshagent-sha256-from-your-approved-build>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Verify whether MeshCentral is an approved RMM for this host/business unit; inspect the file path, SHA256 (reputation), signer, and the parent process that dropped it. 2) Contain: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the MeshAgent service/process, and block its outbound WSS destination at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: Search other hosts for the same SHA256/service, look for co-located ransomware staging (rclone.exe, GPO logon scripts, .SINOBI files) and enumerate the account that installed the service.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "meshagent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "MeshAgent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "MeshCentral"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Mesh Agent\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "meshagent"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\Program Files\Mesh Agent\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment (Warlock / Storm-2603 ransomware) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of Zoho Assist Unattended Agent binaries, the RMM tool Warlock (Storm-2603) operators install for persistent, session-independent remote control ahead of encryption. Flags the agent/installer binaries especially when run non-interactively or as SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the corroborated report detail that Warlock/Storm-2603 deployed the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for persistence; the unattended/SYSTEM context distinguishes attacker deployment from interactive helpdesk use. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026 and Intel471 RMM-abuse writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/understanding-and-threat-hunting-for-rmm-software-misuse
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Zoho Assist use by an internal or outsourced IT helpdesk
  • MSP performing legitimate unattended-access provisioning
  • Software inventory/patching workflows that bundle Zoho
  • User-initiated Zoho support session for a real ticket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("helpdesk-svc","msp-support") and DeviceName !in~ ("<known-helpdesk-hosts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether Zoho Assist is an approved support tool for this host; check who initiated it, the parent process, and whether an unattended (session-independent) install was performed. 2) Contain: If unauthorized, isolate the host, remove the Zoho Assist Unattended service, and block Zoho Assist gateway domains for the affected segment. 3) Hunt: Enumerate other hosts with the same binary/service, review for follow-on ransomware TTPs (rclone staging, shadow-copy deletion, GPO logon scripts) and audit the service account used for install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ZOHO"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Zoho Assist"
    or FileName in~ ("ZA_Access.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZMAgent.exe")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho_Assist"

Email-hiding inbox rules created post-compromise (BEC / mailbox concealment) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts creation/modification of Exchange Online inbox rules that delete, mark-as-read, redirect, or move messages to hidden folders — the concealment step Talos IR observed after auth-abuse account takeover, often preceding large outbound email bursts. Distinct from generic phishing-click detections. Rationale: Grounds on the corroborated Talos IR finding of email-hiding rule creation (T1564.008) and outbound-email spikes after auth abuse; scoping to delete/redirect/mark-read parameters keeps only concealment-intent rules rather than benign filing rules. Cross-checked Talos IR Q2 2026. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately auto-filing newsletters into folders or Deleted Items
  • Executive assistant configuring forwarding to a shared mailbox
  • Mailbox migration/cleanup tooling that rewrites rules in bulk
  • Out-of-office or VIP triage rules marking mail as read
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("DeleteMessage","ForwardTo","RedirectTo","Deleted Items"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the rule parameters and the creating IP/UserAgent against the user's baseline; check if the same session had a risky/device-code sign-in or impossible travel. 2) Contain: If malicious, remove the inbox rule, revoke sessions, reset credentials + re-register MFA, and search sent items for fraudulent/BEC messages. 3) Hunt: Correlate with outbound email volume spikes (e.g., thousands of messages), other users with identical rule patterns, and OAuth app consents from the same source IP.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Exchange Online"
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules","Update-InboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| where Parameters has_any ("DeleteMessage","Deleted Items","MarkAsRead","Junk Email","MoveToFolder","ForwardTo","RedirectTo")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, OfficeWorkload, Parameters
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

let LookbackDays = 7d;

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "fc18d4060c6dad3057c0b5a70a2081473e066951720cafbd2aa159d3aaccf2e1", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "ded73d04bb3e3525226de64c38a332e3", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT

Flyto2 flyto-verification unauthenticated POST /run on :8344 (CVE-2026-67426 SSRF entry) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST to the /run endpoint of the flyto-verification service on TCP 8344 from non-loopback/remote sources. The shipped Dockerfile binds 0.0.0.0:8344 and /run has no auth dependency, so any remote POST /run is the unauthenticated entry point for the callback_url SSRF and runner-secret exfiltration chain. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete endpoint (POST /run) and the Dockerfile-shipped port 8344 (verification_service.py:363-364, Dockerfile.verification CMD). Restricting to external/remote sources leverages the fix guidance ('bind loopback by default') to separate attack traffic from legit internal callers. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory confirming the 0.0.0.0:8344 exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-67426
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal verification jobs POSTing /run from an app tier reachable via a public NAT egress IP
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tools probing the /run path on 8344
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting /run
  • Developer testing the verification service from a bastion/VPN with a public source IP
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("<known-healthcheck-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not an expected internal caller; pull the full request (body should contain callback_url/workflowYaml) from app or proxy logs and check whether the host is running flyto-core <= 2.26.6. 2) Contain: rebind flyto-verification to loopback (or firewall 8344 to internal only), and rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET immediately since it may already be exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 — search for outbound connections from the verification host to 169.254.169.254 or to any public IP, and audit engine-callback authentications using the (now-possibly-leaked) runner secret.

| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog

flyto-verification SSRF to cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) — runner-secret/IMDS theft AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound connections from the flyto-verification runner (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/flyto-verification) to cloud instance-metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200, metadata.google.internal). CVE-2026-67426's callback_url bypasses the target_allowed allowlist and SSRF guard, letting an attacker force the service to POST to the IMDS with a controlled body and harvest instance credentials. Rationale: The article explicitly names 'cloud-metadata IP' as an SSRF target; MITRE T1552.005 and Elastic's prebuilt IMDS-SSRF rule confirm 169.254.169.254 (plus Alibaba 100.100.100.200 / GCP metadata.google.internal) as the canonical endpoints. Scoping to the python/flyto-verification process removes legit cloud-agent IMDS calls, making a web-runner->IMDS connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/credential_access_web_server_cloud_imds_ssrf_request • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate flyto workflow that intentionally targets an internal 169.254.x host as a callback (rare/misconfig)
  • Cloud SDK embedded in the same python venv making a genuine IMDSv2 token call for the app's own role
  • Security testing / red-team validation of the SSRF fix
  • Sidecar or observability agent sharing the process name 'python' reaching metadata for instance tags
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flyto", "verification")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is the flyto-verification runner and capture the destination path/body; check IMDS access logs (if IMDSv2 enabled) for a token issuance from this host at the same time. 2) Contain: rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET and any instance-role credentials that IMDS could have returned; enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) and block 169.254.0.0/16 egress from the container; upgrade flyto-core to 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/AAD/GCP audit for use of the instance-role or managed-identity credentials from unexpected IPs shortly after this event, and check UC3 for the secret being POSTed to an external attacker host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "flyto-verification", "flyto")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or DstHostname has "metadata.google.internal"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification runner egress to external public host — FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the flyto-verification/python runner initiating outbound connections to public (non-RFC1918, non-link-local) destinations. Because callback_url is attacker-controlled and the service unconditionally attaches X-Internal-Key: $FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, any egress from this backend runner to an arbitrary internet host is a candidate secret-exfiltration callback. Rationale: Grounded in the sink from the advisory: post_callback -> session.post(callback_url, headers={'X-Internal-Key': FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET}) (verification_service.py:330-335). A backend verification runner that is only supposed to call the internal engine should never egress to a public IP, so process-scoped public egress is a high-value exfiltration hunt for the leaked runner secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jx74-cqjv-2c67 • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-67428
ATT&CKT1567 T1552
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate engine callback endpoint hosted on a public IP / SaaS domain rather than internal
  • Python dependency/package fetches (pip, telemetry SDKs) from the same runner venv
  • Outbound calls to a public webhook/notification service used by real workflows
  • CDN or object-storage uploads the workflow performs as designed
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "pypi.org" and RemoteUrl !has "pythonhosted.org"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the public RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and compare against the documented internal engine callback host; if it is unknown/attacker-looking, capture the flow and any TLS SNI. 2) Contain: block egress from the flyto-verification container except to the known engine, rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, and upgrade to flyto-core 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (inbound POST /run carrying that callback_url) and UC2 (IMDS access), and review engine-callback auth logs for forged authenticated callbacks using the leaked X-Internal-Key.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("flyto-verification", "flyto")) or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flyto")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"

OctLurk deployment via 'GoogleUpDate' scheduled task launching Videos\1.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the OctLurk/LurkProxy deployment step where the actor creates a scheduled task named GoogleUpDate that runs a staging batch script from the user's Videos or Desktop folder to install the loader service. Anchored on the exact task name, batch paths and the two published batch-script MD5s. Rationale: Uses the verbatim task name 'GoogleUpDate' from the article code block, the exact staging paths C:\Users\<user>\Videos\1.bat and Desktop\auto.bat, and the two published batch MD5s (6ecf84... and b874123...) — all attacker-chosen, high-fidelity strings. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google Update/Chrome update scheduled tasks named 'GoogleUpdateTaskMachine' (note different casing/spacing — GoogleUpDate is the impostor)
  • Admin-authored batch scripts stored under a user's Videos or Desktop folder for ad-hoc automation
  • Software-deployment tooling that stages .bat files on Desktop before running
  • Pen-test/red-team tooling using schtasks for lateral execution
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceProcessEvents tree on the host — confirm the task ran as SYSTEM immediately after creation and whether it invoked sc.exe/1.bat to create a service (NgcCIntSvc/Cusrxsrv/etc.). 2) Contain: delete the GoogleUpDate task, isolate the host, and capture the referenced .bat and any DLL it drops for hashing against the loader IOCs. 3) Hunt: sweep for the loader service names and C2 domain dns.multitoconference.com across the estate; check which admin account created the task (remote creation implies stolen creds).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Desktop\auto.bat"
    or MD5 in ("6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a","b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6")
    or InitiatingProcessMD5 in ("6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a","b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or CommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
    or CommandLine has @"\Desktop\auto.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/LurkProxy loader service registration (ServiceMain=RegisterService loading oleasapi.dll/msbasesysdc.dll) AIInstallation High
Hunts the loader install step where a service is created whose ServiceMain parameter is set to the export 'RegisterService' and whose ServiceDll is one of the named loader DLLs. Covers the custom loader execution/payload-decryption stage flagged by the reviewer. Rationale: Anchors on the article's distinctive loader mechanics: ServiceMain param pointing at the non-standard export 'RegisterService', the exact loader DLL names oleasapi.dll (MD5 082d49ef...) and msbasesysdc.dll, and the attacker-chosen service names. Legit service DLLs almost never store 'RegisterService' as ServiceMain. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1055.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Hyper-V integration services (vmicvss, vmictimesync) — note the impostor is vmictimerosync/vmicagent with altered spelling
  • Genuine PNRPHostSvc / peer-networking service reconfiguration (excluded from the name list for this reason)
  • Third-party service-DLL products that legitimately set a custom ServiceMain export name
  • Backup/EDR agents re-registering service DLLs during upgrade
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryKey has @"\Services\vmictimesync" or RegistryKey has @"\Services\vmicvss")
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host dump the service registry key and the referenced DLL; hash it against 082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069 and check for the RegisterService/Refresh exports. 2) Contain: stop and delete the malicious service, isolate the host, and preserve the DLL and the C: volume serial (used as loader XOR key-2). 3) Hunt: pivot from the DLL to svchost network connections toward the LurkProxy/OctLurk C2 IPs and to any GoogleUpDate task; sweep other hosts for the same service names.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceMain" and RegistryValueData =~ "RegisterService")
    or (RegistryValueName in~ ("ServiceDll","ImagePath") and RegistryValueData has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll"))
    or RegistryKey has_any (@"\Services\NgcCIntSvc", @"\Services\Cusrxsrv", @"\Services\specitsrc", @"\Services\cmtastsvc", @"\Services\vmictimerosync", @"\Services\vmicagent")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceFileName has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
    or ServiceName in~ ("NgcCIntSvc","Cusrxsrv","specitsrc","cmtastsvc","vmictimerosync","vmicagent")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to named backdoor infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host communication with the published OctLurk, SilkLurk and LurkProxy C2 domains and IP addresses (many on dynamic-DNS providers, backdoor sockets on TCP/443). High-fidelity IOC match tying an endpoint to the campaign's command-and-control. Rationale: Direct match on the article's Indicators-of-Compromise section: 15 C2 domains (incl. dynamic-DNS gleeze.com/kozow.com/casacam.net/accesscam.org used by the backdoors) and 11 C2 IPs, including dns.multitoconference.com (OctLurk, TCP/443) and 154.196.162.76 (LurkProxy). Projecting InitiatingProcessFileName surfaces the svchost/service host that beacons. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com is a lookalike of a real retailer domain — a genuine visit to the retailer's real domain will not match this exact FQDN, but analysts may confuse the two
  • Security scanners / TI-enrichment sandboxes deliberately resolving IOC domains
  • Threat-intel researchers detonating samples in the same tenant
  • Recycled dynamic-DNS hostnames later re-registered by benign users (low, but possible for gleeze/kozow subdomains)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the beaconing host — expect svchost.exe hosting a malicious service DLL rather than a browser. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at egress and DNS sinkhole, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: from the host pivot to the loader service (UC2) and GoogleUpDate task (UC1), pull all other internal hosts resolving the same DDNS providers, and review any Impacket/FSCAN activity that may have followed C2 established.

OctLurk victim-fingerprinting recon command burst (chcp 1256 + qwinsta + klist + tasklist) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-compromise fingerprinting sequence OctLurk runs through its command shell plugin: switching the code page to 1256 (Arabic), enumerating sessions with qwinsta, listing Kerberos logon sessions with klist sessions, and running TASKLIST /V — several fired from one parent within minutes. Rationale: Built from the article's exact fingerprinting command table (chcp 1256, powershell $PSVersionTable, qwinsta, klist sessions, TASKLIST /V). chcp 1256 (Arabic code page, matching the Syrian/MoFA victimology) plus the burst of session/process discovery from a single parent within 10 minutes is far more specific than any single LOLBin. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1082 T1057 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/sysadmin interactively troubleshooting RDP sessions (qwinsta) and Kerberos (klist) on a server
  • Logon scripts that call chcp for localization on Arabic-locale endpoints
  • Monitoring/inventory agents running tasklist /V periodically
  • PowerShell profiling scripts querying $PSVersionTable during onboarding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mmc.exe","explorer.exe","taskmgr.exe","ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process of the command burst — a cmd.exe spawned by svchost/an unknown service DLL (not an interactive shell) strongly indicates the OctLurk command-shell plugin. 2) Contain: if parent is a suspicious service host, isolate and capture the DLL. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/timeframe with C2 beacons (UC3) and follow-on credential dumping (UC5) or FSCAN (UC6); check whether chcp 1256 aligns with Arabic-language victim targeting.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "chcp.com" and ProcessCommandLine has "1256")
    or FileName =~ "qwinsta.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "klist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "sessions")
    or (FileName =~ "tasklist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/V")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize CmdCount=dcount(FileName), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), StartTime=min(Timestamp), EndTime=max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where CmdCount >= 3
| order by StartTime desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\chcp.com" and CommandLine has "1256")
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\qwinsta.exe"
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\klist.exe" and CommandLine has "sessions")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\tasklist.exe" and CommandLine has "/V")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize CmdCount=dcount(NewProcessName), Cmds=make_set(CommandLine, 10), StartTime=min(TimeGenerated), EndTime=max(TimeGenerated)
    by Computer, SubjectUserName, ProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CmdCount >= 3
| order by StartTime desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@CommandLine:*"chcp 1256"* OR @Image:(*\qwinsta.exe OR *\Qwinsta.exe) OR @CommandLine:*"klist sessions"* OR @CommandLine:*"TASKLIST /V"* OR @CommandLine:*PSVersionTable*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/chcp\s+1256|klist\s+sessions|tasklist\s+\/v|\$PSVersionTable/i OR ImageFileName=/\\qwinsta\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as cmds dc(Processes.process_name) as cmdcount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chcp.com AND Processes.process="*1256*") OR Processes.process_name=qwinsta.exe OR (Processes.process_name=klist.exe AND Processes.process="*sessions*") OR (Processes.process_name=tasklist.exe AND Processes.process="*/V*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*PSVersionTable*") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=10m | where cmdcount>=3 | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmds dc(Processes.process_name) as cmdcount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chcp.com AND Processes.process="*1256*") OR Processes.process_name=qwinsta.exe OR (Processes.process_name=klist.exe AND Processes.process="*sessions*") OR (Processes.process_name=tasklist.exe AND Processes.process="*/V*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*PSVersionTable*") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=10m | where cmdcount>=3 | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Impacket secretsdump credential dumping in OctLurk post-compromise AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of Impacket's secretsdump used by the actor for credential dumping (SAM/LSA/NTDS) during lateral movement. Detects the secretsdump invocation and its DCSync-style '-just-dc' argument pattern regardless of interpreter or compiled packaging. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Impacket — secretsdump' in post-compromise credential harvesting. Anchoring on the module name and the DCSync-style '-just-dc ...@target' argument shape catches both python and compiled/renamed Impacket packaging without relying on a hash the report says was unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / authorized penetration tests running Impacket secretsdump
  • AD migration or password-audit tooling that legitimately performs DCSync
  • Security researchers testing Impacket in a lab within the same tenant
  • Backup solutions invoking ntds util (different arg shape — should not match '-just-dc @')
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-adaudit","svc-pwaudit")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the account context; confirm whether '-just-dc' (DCSync against a DC) or SAM/LSA local dump, and whether the target host is a domain controller. 2) Contain: isolate source host, force-reset any exposed krbtgt/privileged and service accounts, and revoke Kerberos tickets if DCSync succeeded. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1/UC2 loader presence and UC3 C2 on the same host; look for FSCAN recon (UC6) that preceded the credential dump and unusual admin logons to the DC.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","secretsdump.py")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-just-dc" and ProcessCommandLine has "@")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-just-dc-ntlm" and ProcessCommandLine has "-hashes")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","secretsdump.py")
    or (CommandLine has "-just-dc" and CommandLine has "@")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Impacket secretsdump credential dumping
id: a4e0d2c8-71b6-4f19-9d33-0c6a2e7b4f81

FSCAN internal network reconnaissance fan-out AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the internal reconnaissance stage where the actor runs FSCAN to sweep the network — one source touching many internal hosts across scanner ports (SSH, SMB, RDP, MSSQL, MySQL, Redis) in a short window, plus direct fscan binary execution. Rationale: The article names 'Network scan: FSCAN' as post-compromise activity. Detection combines the direct fscan.exe process (Sigma) with the behavioral fan-out (one internal source hitting >=50 hosts on FSCAN's default scan ports within 5 min), which survives binary renaming. Sentinel query fixed to group on SourceIP/SourceHostName (valid CommonSecurityLog columns) instead of the non-existent DeviceName. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS) sweeping the estate
  • Network/asset-discovery tools (Lansweeper, nmap-based inventory)
  • SCCM/endpoint-management client-push connectivity checks across a subnet
  • Backup or monitoring servers probing SMB/SQL on many hosts
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("scanner01","nessus01","lansweeper01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus-service.exe","nmap.exe","Nessus.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the scanning process (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) and whether the source host is an approved scanner; an unknown/renamed binary spawned by a service host is high-signal for FSCAN. 2) Contain: isolate the source host and block its lateral SMB/RDP/SQL traffic. 3) Hunt: correlate with the loader (UC2), C2 (UC3) and any subsequent secretsdump (UC5); map which internal hosts responded on 445/3389 to scope likely lateral targets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| where RemotePort in (22, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 3306, 3389, 6379)
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(RemoteIP), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20), StartTime=min(Timestamp), EndTime=max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 50   // fscan-style fan-out; tune to /24 estate size
| order by DistinctHosts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort in (22, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 3306, 3389, 6379)
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(DestinationIP), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort, 20), StartTime=min(TimeGenerated), EndTime=max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceIP, SourceHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 50   // fscan-style fan-out; tune to estate size
| order by DistinctHosts desc
title: FSCAN network scanner binary execution

Browser credential-store theft via OctLurk browser password decryptor AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the OctLurk 'Browser Password Decryptor' capability: a non-browser process reading Chromium/Edge 'Login Data' and 'Local State' (AES key) or Firefox 'logins.json'/'key4.db' to steal stored passwords. Rationale: The article lists 'Browser Password Decryptor' / browser password stealer as an OctLurk capability. High-fidelity signal is a non-browser process touching the Chromium 'Login Data' + 'Local State' pair (Local State holds the DPAPI-wrapped AES key) or Firefox key4.db/logins.json — the exact files any browser-credential stealer must read. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty as browser file-read telemetry isn't in their standard sources. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/sync agents (OneDrive, Google Drive, corporate backup) copying user profile directories
  • Endpoint DLP or forensic tools inventorying browser artifacts
  • Browser migration/import utilities reading another browser's profile
  • Antivirus on-access scans opening the SQLite stores
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","googledrivesync.exe","Dropbox.exe","MsMpEng.exe","code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process and its parent; a process from an unusual path or a service host reading both Login Data and Local State is a strong stealer indicator. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force password resets for accounts whose credentials are likely stored in that browser profile (prioritize privileged/SSO). 3) Hunt: correlate with OctLurk loader/C2 on the same host, look for archive utilities (WinRAR/7z) staging the harvested data, and check for outbound transfer to the C2 IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","logins.json","key4.db","Web Data","cookies.sqlite")
    or FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Login Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","OneDrive.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Login Data", @"\User Data\Local State", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
    or TargetFileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","Login Data","Local State")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","msedgewebview2.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-browser access to browser credential stores
